title: Repent, the Fig Tree, and the Narrow Door

verses.text: At that time some of those present told Jesus about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices.
To this He replied, "Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered this way?
No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish.
Or those eighteen who were killed when the tower of Siloam collapsed on them: Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem?
No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish."
Then Jesus told this parable: "A man had a fig tree that was planted in his vineyard. He went to look for fruit on it but did not find any.

So he said to the keeper of the vineyard, 'Look, for the past three years I have come to search for fruit on this fig tree and haven't found any. Therefore cut it down! Why should it use up the soil?'
'Sir,' the man replied, 'leave it alone again this year, until I dig around it and fertilize it.
If it bears fruit next year, fine. But if not, you can cut it down.'"
One Sabbath Jesus was teaching in one of the synagogues,
and a woman there had been disabled by a spirit for eighteen years. She was hunched over and could not stand up straight.
When Jesus saw her, He called her over and said, "Woman, you are set free from your disability."
Then He placed His hands on her, and immediately she straightened up and began to glorify God.
But the synagogue leader was indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath. "There are six days for work," he told the crowd. "So come and be healed on those days and not on the Sabbath."
"You hypocrites!" the Lord replied. "Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or donkey from the stall and lead it to water?
Then should not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has kept bound for eighteen long years, be released from her bondage on the Sabbath day?"
When Jesus said this, all His adversaries were humiliated. And the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things He was doing.
Then Jesus asked, "What is the kingdom of God like? To what can I compare it?
It is like a mustard seed that a man tossed into his garden. It grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air nested in its branches."
Again He asked, "To what can I compare the kingdom of God?
It is like leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour, until all of it was leavened."
Then Jesus traveled throughout the towns and villages, teaching as He made His way toward Jerusalem.
"Lord," someone asked Him, "will only a few people be saved?" Jesus answered,
"Make every effort to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able.
After the master of the house gets up and shuts the door, you will stand outside knocking and saying, 'Lord, open the door for us.' But he will reply, 'I do not know where you are from.'
Then you will say, 'We ate and drank with you, and you taught in our streets.'
And he will answer, 'I tell you, I do not know where you are from. Depart from me, all you evildoers.'
There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth when you see Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but you yourselves are thrown out.
People will come from east and west and north and south, and will recline at the table in the kingdom of God.
And indeed, some who are last will be first, and some who are first will be last.
At that very hour, some Pharisees came to Jesus and told Him, "Leave this place and get away, because Herod wants to kill You."
But Jesus replied, "Go tell that fox, 'Look, I will keep driving out demons and healing people today and tomorrow, and on the third day I will reach My goal.'
Nevertheless, I must keep going today and tomorrow and the next day, for it is not admissible for a prophet to perish outside of Jerusalem.

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!
Look, your house is left to you desolate. And I tell you that you will not see Me again until you say, 'Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.'

context.author: Luke, the physician and companion of Paul
context.genre: Travel narrative with teaching, a Sabbath healing, parables, and a lament, all on the road to Jerusalem
context.audience: Jesus' disciples and the mixed crowds who follow Him, with opponents such as the synagogue leader and some Pharisees listening in. Luke's Gentile readers are shown that standing with God depends on repentance, not on heritage.
context.mapLabel: SILOAM AND THE ROAD TO JERUSALEM
context.setting: Verse 22 says Jesus is "making His way toward Jerusalem," so everything in this chapter happens on the road, in towns and synagogues, with the city and its coming conflict ahead. The tower of Siloam in verse 4 stood by the Pool of Siloam, at the southern end of the city of David, so the disaster was close to home for Jerusalem's people. Galilee was Herod Antipas's territory, which explains why a warning about Herod comes from Pharisees in verse 31.
context.custom: A synagogue leader was responsible for order in the service, so his objection in verse 14 is a real concern for him. Many Jews of the time allowed leading an animal to water on the Sabbath, which is why Jesus' argument in verse 15 lands so hard. At a banquet, to recline at the table (v.29) was to be welcomed as a guest and friend, and to be shut out of the house while others feast inside (v.25-28) was a picture of shame that every hearer understood.
context.timelineImmediate: In Luke 12 Jesus warned the crowd to read the times. Chapter 13 opens with people bringing Him news of a recent atrocity and a recent accident, and He uses both to say that the time to repent is now. The chapter then moves from a final-year parable (v.6-9), to a woman set free (v.10-17), to the kingdom's slow growth (v.18-21), to the narrow door (v.22-30), and ends with Jesus' grief over Jerusalem (v.31-35).
context.timelineBible: Verse 35 quotes Psalm 118:26, the song pilgrims sang at Passover, which the crowds will shout at Jesus' entry into Jerusalem in Luke 19:38. The fig tree gives a new picture of Israel as God's planted vine and tree, as in Isaiah 5 and Jeremiah 8:13. The hen and her chicks echo Psalm 91:4 and Ruth 2:12, where God shelters people under His wings.
context.sparkNotes: Two pieces of bad news prompt Jesus to say that tragedy is not a measure of guilt and that everyone must repent. A fig tree gets one more year, and a woman bent for eighteen years is set free on the Sabbath. Then come the mustard seed and the leaven, a question about whether few are saved, and a door that will not stay open forever. The chapter ends with Jesus refusing to be scared off by Herod and mourning over Jerusalem, which He would have gathered like a hen but which was unwilling.

translation.meaning: Literally to change one's mind. It means a turn of the whole person toward God, not just regret over what happened. Jesus says it twice in the same words, which shows how urgent He thinks it is.
The word means weakness or infirmity. Luke, who was a physician, says the woman was "disabled by a spirit" and could not straighten up at all. In verse 16 Jesus says Satan had kept her bound.
This title gives the woman the dignity of covenant standing in the very synagogue where she was ignored. Jesus sets it against the leader's claim that she should wait for another day.

Tight or restricted. It describes a door that takes effort and cannot be entered while carrying everything with you. The verb "make every effort" is agōnizesthe, from which we get "agonize" and which was used of athletes straining in a contest.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's parables of the mustard seed and the leaven.
Mark's version of the mustard seed.
The narrow gate in the Sermon on the Mount.
"I never knew you; depart from Me" for those who relied on their works and their religious language.
Many will come from east and west to recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, while the sons of the kingdom are thrown out.
The first will be last, and the last first.
The same saying about the first and the last.
Matthew places the lament over Jerusalem in his Jerusalem discourses, with nearly identical words.

otBackground.note: God planted Israel as a vineyard and looked for good fruit. The fig tree parable continues the same image.
A great tree in which the birds of the air nest is a biblical picture of a kingdom with wide shelter, which sits behind the mustard seed parable.
Sarah prepares three measures of flour for her heavenly guests, the same amount used in the leaven parable.
"Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity." Jesus uses the psalmist's words in verse 27.
"Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." The pilgrim song Jesus quotes in verse 35.
God is pictured as an eagle who hovers over its young and spreads its wings, a parallel to the hen and her chicks.

commentary.note: On the Galileans and the tower, Henry draws the line that "we cannot judge of men's sins by their sufferings in this world." Jesus does not explain why bad things happen. He turns the news into a question for the listener: if they perished, you deserve the same, so repent. On the fig tree he reads Israel, and every church that enjoys privileges without bearing fruit. The gardener's request for one more year shows both real mercy and real limits, for God "will not bear always with unfruitful professors."

On the narrow door Henry stresses that the word is "strive," not merely "seek," because many will seek and fail. His sharpest warning is for the people who say they ate and drank with Jesus and heard Him teach, yet are not known by Him. "Many are ruined by an ill-grounded hope of heaven" that they never examined. On the hen and chicks, he says the fault lies wholly with the people, since Christ's willingness "aggravates sinners' unwillingness."

Gill takes the Galileans of verse 1 to be possibly followers of Judas of Galilee, killed by Pilate while sacrificing, so that their blood was literally mingled with the offering. On the bent woman, he says her condition was "brought upon her by an evil spirit, by Satan" with God's permission, and had lasted so long that it was thought incurable. He sees her as a picture of a sinner held in bondage until Christ frees them. On "that fox," he says Jesus names Herod's cunning and subtlety.

Lewis does not comment on Luke 13, but his chapter on hell in The Problem of Pain speaks to the shut door of verses 25-28. He argues that Christ's own words about hell are blunt and that the idea cannot be dropped. He then suggests that the damned are in one sense successful rebels to the end, and that "the doors of hell are locked on the inside." The door in Jesus' parable is shut because the master has stood and closed it, but Lewis's point fits the people outside who insist on their own claim and will not come in on the master's terms. (Paraphrased; Lewis's works remain under copyright.)

overview.summary: Jesus says tragedy is not proof of guilt and calls everyone to repent, then tells of a fig tree given one more year. He frees a bent woman on the Sabbath, warns of a narrow door, and grieves over Jerusalem.
overview.settingLine: Towns and synagogues on the road to Jerusalem.

history.t: Pilate killed Galilean worshipers at their sacrifices, shocking the whole region.
Antipas ruled Galilee and had killed John, so a warning about him was no empty threat.

customs.t: Many Jews allowed leading an animal to water on the Sabbath, which Jesus uses in His answer.
Both were everyday items, so small things growing large was easy to picture.

archaeology.t: The first-century pool was uncovered in 2004, with stone steps used by pilgrims.
A stone found at Caesarea in 1961 names Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judea.

overview.discussion: Jesus said victims of tragedy were no worse sinners than others. How should we think about suffering and blame?
overview.book: The third Gospel · 24 chapters. Written as an orderly account, with Acts as its sequel.
overview.author: Luke
overview.audience: Theophilus and a broad, largely Gentile readership
